claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal nanoparticles can initially exist as a disordered single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy alone does not govern the elevated-temperature stability of high-entropy alloys.
Suppression of brittle intermetallic precipitation is critical to the thermal stability of five-transition-metal HENA.
Suppression of intermetallic precipitation acts as a kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion or phase separation.
A local atomic-radius difference above 6.4% causes loss of single-phase stability.
A sufficiently negative mixing enthalpy drives spontaneous ordering.
Annealing at 900–1600 °C is sufficient to activate atomic diffusion in the proposed nanoparticles.
Reducing particle size increases surface-to-volume effects relevant to structural evolution.
Oxidation alters surface-diffusion kinetics, so vacuum or an inert atmosphere is required to isolate intrinsic behavior.
Particle sizes below 100 nm maximize surface-energy contributions.
Ordered B2-type and brittle C14 Laves precipitates can occur in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Brittle W-enriched BCC phases occur in conventional W-based alloys and contribute to poor mechanical-property balance.
Ordered or brittle precipitates accelerate atomic diffusion through grain boundaries or precipitate–matrix interfaces.
Configurational entropy greater than 1.5R theoretically stabilizes a solid solution.
Severe atomic-size mismatch or negative mixing enthalpy causes nucleation of brittle ordered phases.
Violation of δ ≤ 6.4% and −20 ≤ ΔH_mix ≤ 5 kJ/mol will produce rapid evolution from a single-phase nanoparticle to a multiphase structure.
The resulting multiphase nanoparticles will lose thermal stability and mechanical strength relative to bulk counterparts.
Traditional W-alloy design uses dilute additions such as Re, Ti, and Cr to improve properties.
For δ below 2%, configurational entropy completely dominates stability.
Above a particle size of 1 µm, surface energy no longer significantly alters the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes suppression of intermetallic precipitation as a kinetic barrier, whereas the mediator and mechanism state that formation of precipitates accelerates diffusion. The identity and direction of the proposed kinetic barrier are therefore inconsistent.

The target is repeatedly described as a five-transition-metal alloy, but NbMoTaW is offered as an example even though it contains only four elements. NbMoTaTiV is the only listed five-element example.
